# Diagnosing No Heat in a 2006 Chevy Equinox: Beyond the Heater Core

When a 2006 Chevy Equinox fails to produce cabin heat after replacing the dash door (blend door actuator) and the thermostat, the problem almost certainly shifts from airflow distribution or coolant flow regulation to a blockage or a lack of pressure. The fact that the mechanic replaced the heater core is less likely to be the culpritâsource material confirms they verified it wasn't the issueâand adds coolant without immediate leaks suggests the integrity of the sealing surfaces is intact, but not necessarily that the system is functional under load.

In automotive cooling systems, heat transfer relies on a specific thermodynamic sequence: the engine must generate sufficient excess heat to push fluid through the heater core before it can be circulated into the cabin. If the thermostat was replaced but the system still lacks heat, we must verify whether the thermostat itself is actually opening at its rated temperature (typically 195Â°F for this generation GM platform) or if it remains stuck closed due to a manufacturing defect in the new unit. A stuck-closed thermostat prevents coolant from reaching the heater core entirely because the engine bay becomes too hot to allow reverse flow, but the radiator side remains cool.

If the mechanic has already replaced the actuator and confirmed the heater core isn't physically plugged, the next logical step is checking for an air lock. Air locks are insidious; they form pockets of gas that block liquid flow. Even if you see coolant in the reservoir, a large air pocket can sit directly over the heater core inlet nipple on the firewall. This prevents hot coolant from entering the core, leaving only cold coolant circulating through it. To resolve this, you need to physically purge the system while the engine is running at operating temperature.

One effective method involves locating the bleed screw on the upper radiator hose or using a specialized vacuum filler funnel if one isn't already installed. With the engine running and the heater set to maximum heat and fan high, slowly open the bleed point until a steady stream of coolant bubbles out without interruption. If the system lacks a dedicated bleed screw, raising the vehicle and carefully opening the lower radiator cap while the engine is warm (but not boiling) can allow trapped air to escape through the filler neck.

Another critical component often overlooked in 2006 Equinox models is the water pump impeller. Many of these units utilize plastic impellers that degrade over time, causing cavitation or reduced flow rate. If the pump is failing to circulate enough volume of coolant, the heater core receives insufficient thermal energy to warm the cabin air, even if the thermostat is open and the actuator is moving correctly. You can test this by feeling the temperature difference between the upper and lower radiator hoses while idling with the AC off and heater on. If both hoses are cold, the pump is not circulating fluid effectively.

Finally, consider the HVAC blend door location. While the "dash door" mentioned in the source material usually refers to the actuator motor, the physical plastic flap itself can become warped or detached from its track. If the flap is stuck in the cold-air position due to mechanical binding in the slider guides, replacing the motor will not help. Inspect the plenum box for any visible damage or misalignment that prevents the door from reaching the full "heat" position.
